shortQuestions: The Quaid said the Constituent Assembly had two main functions: first, to frame the future constitution of Pakistan, and second, to work as a full and sovereign legislative body (the Federal Legislature) for the country until the constitution was made.

He meant the creation of two independent states, Pakistan and India, in the subcontinent. He called it unprecedented because there was no parallel in history of such a vast change — the creation of a new state by peaceful democratic struggle and the transfer of power over so many millions of people.

He called bribery and corruption a poison and one of the biggest curses, which must be put down with an iron hand. He also condemned black-marketing as a great crime, and called nepotism and jobbery an evil inherited from the past that he would not tolerate.

He said that many people did not agree with the partition of India, but in his opinion there was no other solution; a united India would never have worked and would have led to disaster. Partition was a final settlement that both sides should honour, and history would prove it right.

In the Quaid's view the biggest hindrance was the class and communal division — the division between Hindus and Muslims (and the castes among Hindus); without these divisions India would have won freedom long ago.

He assured the minorities of full equality: every citizen, whatever his religion, caste or creed, would have equal rights, privileges and obligations. Minorities would be protected and free to practise their religion; the state would not discriminate against anyone on the basis of faith.

He envisioned freedom of religion and worship, equality of citizenship, freedom from fear, corruption and exploitation — "You are free to go to your temples, mosques or any other places of worship", with religion being a personal matter of the individual and not the business of the state.

He did not mean that people would give up their faith. He meant that in the political sense, as citizens of the state, people would not be treated as Hindus or Muslims; religious identity would remain a personal matter, while all would be equal citizens of Pakistan.

His vision was of a democratic, welfare state based on justice, equality and fair play; free from corruption, bribery and nepotism; where all citizens, including minorities, have equal rights and religious freedom; and where the people work with unity, faith and discipline for the progress and prosperity of the nation.

His guiding principles were justice and complete impartiality — he said he would be guided by fair play and would not be swayed by any political or party prejudice in his position as President, and he asked for the cooperation of all for this. Significance: these principles are the foundation of good government — they build trust in the state, protect the rights of all citizens, unite the nation and make the rule of law possible.
activities: Debate points — the Pakistan the Quaid wanted: a democratic state where sovereignty belongs to Allah and authority is used by the people's representatives; based on the principles of Islam — justice, equality and brotherhood; a welfare state free from corruption, bribery, black-marketing and nepotism; equal rights and religious freedom for minorities; unity, faith and discipline as national values; economic independence and education. Each group should support its arguments with quotations from the Quaid's speeches (11 August 1947 and others).

Sample essay — Quaid-e-Azam was a far-sighted political leader. (Hook) Few leaders in history created a nation and a state at the same time. (Thesis) The Quaid's speech of 11 August 1947 shows his far-sightedness. Body: (1) He saw that a united India would not have worked and accepted partition as the only solution. (2) He named the dangers the new state would face — bribery, corruption, black-marketing, nepotism — and asked for them to be crushed with an iron hand. (3) He knew that a stable state needs the trust of all citizens, so he promised equal rights and religious freedom to minorities. (4) He gave the Assembly a double role — making the constitution and governing the country. Conclusion: His vision of a just, democratic and united Pakistan is still the best guide for the nation.
